slides.headline: Rome’s Conquest Colony Became the Conquered
slides.subheadline: Discover how Tipasa became ruins—and why modern Tipaza begins another chapter.
slides.svgBlueprint: Use a 1080×1350 portrait viewBox and 80px safe margins. Inherit this canvas and palette throughout. Place the publication masthead above a thin ink rule; wrap the accent-outlined kicker across two lines. Set the headline at 68px in three monumental lines. Below, draw one abstract column severed by a red diagonal gap: an editorial emblem, not an archaeological reconstruction. Place the 30px subheadline beneath it. Align two compact date badges along the bottom, with the issue badge in the footer. No diagrams, cards, arrows, or callouts.

slides.headline: The Conquest Base Becomes a Target
slides.subheadline: Vandal destruction reverses the fortunes of Rome’s former military colony.

items.label: Before the rupture
items.body: Colonia Aelia Tipasensis reached 20,000 inhabitants, according to Stéphane Gsell.

items.label: The reversal
items.body: Vandal forces destroyed Tipasa: the settlement once serving conquest was itself conquered.

slides.svgBlueprint: Set the 56px headline above two vertically stacked milestones. Draw a narrow ink spine through the upper surface panel, then interrupt it with a broad red gap before the lower panel. Display the upper period badge at 30px and the lower date at 56px. Keep each body at 30px within a 740px text measure. Use no population-scaled shapes: the contrast represents historical reversal, not measured destruction.

slides.headline: More Than a Roman Military Outpost
slides.subheadline: A conquest base became a populous city and an important Christian hub.

items.label: Fourth-century population
items.body: Stéphane Gsell’s estimate gives the colony a human scale beyond its military purpose.

items.label: Christian hub
items.body: Religious buildings marked Tipasa’s importance during the last centuries of Roman governorship.

slides.svgBlueprint: Place the 56px headline and 30px subheadline above a full-width population placard. Set only '20,000' at 84px; place 'inhabitants' underneath at 30px. Keep the fourth-century label and Gsell attribution adjacent. Below, use one surface footnote card containing three simple arch outlines and the exact badge 'three basilicas'. Add a restrained red baseline. The arches are symbolic, not reconstructed building plans.

slides.headline: Destruction Meets an Imperial Rebuilding Project
slides.subheadline: Vandal destruction and Byzantine reconstruction pulled the city in opposing directions.

items.label: Vandal destruction
items.body: The city was destroyed; Roman imperial ownership had offered no permanent protection.

items.label: Byzantine reconstruction
items.body: The Byzantines reconstructed Tipasa, restoring buildings without guaranteeing the city’s survival.

slides.svgBlueprint: Under the full-width heading, divide the canvas into equal vertical panels separated by a 4px red rule. Use ink with paper text on the left and surface with ink text on the right. Draw abstract fallen blocks opposite an outlined standing arch. Cap date numerals at 52px and render 'one century later' at 32px over two lines. Wrap bodies at 28px. Mark the panels 'DESTRUCTION' and 'RECONSTRUCTION'; do not imply simultaneous armies or a direct battle.

slides.headline: Rebuilding Was Not the Final Chapter
slides.subheadline: Another demolition separates the ancient city’s history from modern Tipaza’s founding.

items.label: Umayyad demolition
items.body: Umayyad forces demolished the city and reduced it to ruins.

items.label: A separate founding
items.body: Modern Tipaza was founded during nineteenth-century resettlement, not through uninterrupted ancient urban continuity.

slides.svgBlueprint: Place the ancient milestone on a lower-left surface step and the modern founding on an upper-right paper step. Separate them with conspicuous blank space and a broken red connector. Label the connector 'CHRONOLOGY, NOT TO SCALE'. Render the complete ancient period badge at 28px across three lines; set 1857 at 56px. Keep bodies at 28px and preserve clear reading order with a subtle upward arrow. Never depict a continuous skyline across the gap.

slides.headline: Two Populations, Not One Continuous City
slides.subheadline: The population figures describe different settlements, not a continuous growth story.

items.label: Ancient Tipasa
items.body: Stéphane Gsell’s fourth-century estimate measures inhabitants, not casualties from later conquests.

items.label: Modern Tipaza
items.body: A modern population description, not a dated census or evidence of uninterrupted settlement.

slides.svgBlueprint: Use two full-width cards of unequal height, offset horizontally by 40px. Give the ancient card an ink border and the modern card a surface fill with a red edge. Set population numerals at 56px; keep 'nearly' visibly attached to 30,000 and units on their own lines. Place attribution and period directly beneath the ancient figure. Do not use proportional bars, a percentage change, casualty symbols, or a connecting growth arrow.

slides.headline: Imperial Ruins Become the Modern Draw
slides.subheadline: The conquest base now attracts visitors. Who protects what remains?​

items.label: Modern town founded
items.body: Tipaza’s appeal rests principally on ancient ruins, alongside its sandy littoral.

items.label: World Heritage inscription
items.body: Tipasa’s protected remains face pressures from urban development, unregulated tourism and population growth.

Make the first card paper with an ink rule; make the second surface with a red conservation marker. Finish with 'The Zurich Typographer · tipaza.pub' and generous negative space.
